reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: The defining feature is bilateral pitting oedema, which can mask underlying wasting and lead to underestimation of the severity of malnutrition
Other signs include a distended abdomen with fatty liver, sparse depigmented hair, flaky-paint dermatosis, apathy, and irritability
It typically affects young children after weaning onto a starchy, protein-poor diet, often precipitated by an intercurrent infection
It remains relevant in parts of India and other low-income settings, particularly in food-insecure and displaced populations
Affected children are immunodeficient, so infection is common, frequently without fever, and is a leading cause of death
Feeding must follow a cautious, staged protocol because rapid refeeding risks fatal metabolic and cardiac complications
Hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbance must be actively sought and corrected
reference.pathophysiology: Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition in which protein deficiency is relatively greater than energy deficiency. Reduced hepatic synthesis of albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, and this, together with increased capillary permeability, sodium retention, and oxidative stress, produces the characteristic oedema. Fatty infiltration of the liver reflects impaired lipoprotein export. Loss of immune competence, gut mucosal atrophy, and micronutrient deficiencies compound the picture, and metabolic adaptation to starvation makes the child vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, and dangerous fluid and electrolyte shifts during treatment.
additionalDifferentials: Nephrotic syndrome causing oedema and hypoalbuminaemia
Chronic liver disease with ascites and oedema
additionalInvestigations: Anthropometry with weight-for-height and mid-upper-arm circumference, and assessment for oedema
Blood glucose to detect hypoglycaemia and temperature to detect hypothermia
Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, and phosphate
Screening for infection, which is often occult
Assessment for micronutrient deficiencies and anaemia
redFlags: Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, which are life-threatening in severe malnutrition
Signs of sepsis, which may present without fever
Circulatory or cardiac failure and danger of fluid overload with rehydration
Refeeding-related electrolyte shifts during early nutritional rehabilitation
reference.prognosis: With careful staged nutritional rehabilitation and treatment of infection, recovery is possible, but mortality is high when complications such as sepsis, hypoglycaemia, or refeeding are not anticipated and managed.
pitfalls: Underestimating malnutrition because oedema masks wasting
Refeeding too aggressively and precipitating cardiac failure or refeeding syndrome
Overzealous intravenous rehydration causing fluid overload
Missing occult infection because the usual signs of fever and inflammation are blunted
management: Follow a cautious, staged nutritional rehabilitation protocol, beginning with a low-protein, low-energy stabilisation formula before transitioning to catch-up feeding, to avoid fatal refeeding syndrome
Detect and correct hypoglycaemia and hypothermia promptly with frequent feeds and active warming
Restore electrolytes with potassium and magnesium and give cautious rehydration to avoid fluid overload and cardiac failure
Treat presumed infection empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics because sepsis is often occult and afebrile
Provide micronutrient replacement including vitamin A, zinc and folate, deferring iron until the recovery phase
Attend to the flaky-paint dermatosis with gentle skin care and manage the oedema
Arrange multidisciplinary follow-up with caregiver education and measures to address the underlying food insecurity
Escalate to inpatient or high-dependency care for signs of shock, worsening oedema or feeding intolerance
